reference.source: Moss and Adams' Heart Disease in Infants, Children, and Adolescents
clinicalPearls: Heterotaxy describes abnormal arrangement of thoraco-abdominal organs across the left-right axis that is neither normal (situs solitus) nor complete mirror-image (situs inversus), reflecting failure to establish normal asymmetry.

It is broadly divided into right atrial isomerism (asplenia, bilateral right-sidedness) and left atrial isomerism (polysplenia, bilateral left-sidedness), each with characteristic cardiac and visceral patterns.
Complex congenital heart disease is the rule rather than the exception, so any infant with discordant visceral situs on imaging needs urgent detailed echocardiography.
Bronchial and atrial appendage morphology are the most reliable anatomical markers of isomerism, more dependable than spleen number alone.
Right isomerism tends to produce severe cyanotic lesions with common atrioventricular canal, single ventricle and anomalous pulmonary venous drainage, often with functional asplenia.
Left isomerism is associated with polysplenia, interruption of the inferior vena cava with azygos continuation, biliary atresia and heart block from an abnormal or absent sinus node.
Intestinal malrotation is common in both forms, and an apparently well child can present acutely with midgut volvulus.
Functional asplenia mandates lifelong sepsis prophylaxis and vaccination, while conduction disease in left isomerism may require pacing.
reference.pathophysiology: Heterotaxy results from disruption of the molecular pathways that normally break embryonic left-right symmetry. Motile cilia at the primitive node generate leftward nodal flow that is sensed by peripheral immotile cilia, triggering asymmetric activation of the Nodal-Lefty-Pitx2 cascade that instructs sidedness of the heart, gut, spleen and vasculature. When this signalling fails, organ primordia default towards a symmetric or randomised state, so paired structures adopt the same morphology on both sides (isomerism) rather than distinct left and right patterns. Bilateral right-sidedness produces morphologically right structures duplicated (trilobed lungs, eparterial bronchi, absent spleen, midline liver), typically with severe conotruncal and atrioventricular septal defects. Bilateral left-sidedness produces duplicated left structures (bilobed lungs, hyparterial bronchi, multiple spleens, interrupted inferior vena cava) with a tendency to conduction abnormalities. Many cases involve ciliary or laterality gene defects, linking heterotaxy mechanistically to the ciliopathy spectrum.
additionalDifferentials: situs solitus with isolated congenital heart disease
additionalInvestigations: detailed segmental echocardiography including venous and atrial appendage assessment
abdominal ultrasound for spleen number, hepatic symmetry and vascular anatomy
chest radiograph and cross-sectional imaging for bronchial morphology and situs
peripheral blood film for Howell-Jolly bodies indicating functional asplenia
cardiac MRI or CT angiography for complex venous and arterial connections
twelve-lead ECG and Holter monitoring for conduction disease and heart block
genetic evaluation for laterality and ciliopathy genes
redFlags: neonatal cyanosis or shock from duct-dependent complex congenital heart disease
bilious vomiting suggesting midgut volvulus from associated malrotation
fever or overwhelming sepsis in a child with functional asplenia
bradycardia or syncope from complete heart block in left isomerism
progressive jaundice raising concern for associated biliary atresia
reference.prognosis: Outcome is dictated by the severity of associated cardiac malformation and, in right isomerism, by the added risk of overwhelming infection from asplenia; right isomerism generally carries the poorer prognosis. Multidisciplinary cardiac surgical staging, malrotation surveillance and infection prophylaxis substantially improve survival though many require complex single-ventricle palliation.
pitfalls: Relying on spleen number rather than bronchial and atrial appendage morphology to classify isomerism.
Missing intestinal malrotation until the child presents with volvulus.
Failing to institute antibiotic prophylaxis and vaccination in functional asplenia.
Overlooking inferior vena cava interruption during central line placement or catheterisation.
Underappreciating progressive conduction disease in left isomerism.

management: Manage the complex congenital heart disease with staged surgical palliation or repair, often along a single-ventricle Fontan pathway, guided by detailed segmental echocardiography

In right isomerism with asplenia or functional asplenia, give lifelong antibiotic prophylaxis, vaccinate against encapsulated organisms, and treat any febrile illness urgently as possible overwhelming sepsis
Screen for and surgically correct intestinal malrotation with a Ladd procedure to prevent midgut volvulus
In left isomerism, evaluate for biliary atresia requiring a Kasai portoenterostomy and for sinus node dysfunction or heart block requiring pacing
Undertake surveillance with serial echocardiography and ECG or Holter monitoring for arrhythmia and conduction disease
Coordinate multidisciplinary care across paediatric cardiology, cardiac surgery, general surgery and immunology, and offer genetic counselling
Escalate immediately for any febrile episode in an asplenic patient given the risk of fulminant infection
